pyqs.question_text: Let X and Y be independent random variables with exponential distribution having respective means 1/lambda_1 and 1/lambda_2, lambda_1 > 0, lambda_2 > 0. Find E[max(X, Y)].
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must first write the CDF of max(X,Y) as the product of the individual exponential CDFs, then obtain the density of max(X,Y) by differentiation. Full marks require correctly integrating x times this density (or using E[max]=E[X]+E[Y]-E[min] with E[min]=1/(lambda_1+lambda_2)) to reach the closed-form answer 1/lambda_1 + 1/lambda_2 - 1/(lambda_1+lambda_2). Partial credit for a correct CDF/density setup without full simplification.

pyqs.question_text: Using the Central Limit Theorem, show that the limit as n tends to infinity of e^(-n) times the sum from k=0 to n of n^k/k! equals 1/2.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must recognise the sum as P(X_n <= n) for X_n Poisson(n), which can be represented as a sum of n i.i.d. unit-mean Poisson variables. Candidate should standardise (X_n - n)/sqrt(n) and apply the CLT to show this converges in distribution to standard normal, so P(X_n <= n) tends to Phi(0) = 1/2. Full marks require explicitly identifying the Poisson-as-sum-of-Poissons device and the correct standardisation; no credit for merely asserting the result.

pyqs.question_text: An unbiased six-sided die is thrown twice. Let X denote the smaller of the two scores obtained. Show that the probability mass function of X is given by p_X(x) = (13 - 2x)/36 for x = 1, 2, ..., 6, and 0 otherwise.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate should compute P(X >= x) = P(both throws >= x) = ((7-x)/6)^2 for each x, then obtain p_X(x) = P(X>=x) - P(X>=x+1) and simplify algebraically to (13-2x)/36. Full marks require the complete derivation with correct simplification and a check that probabilities sum to 1; partial credit for a correct enumeration-based verification without the general algebraic form.

pyqs.question_text: Out of 1000 persons born, only 900 reach the age of 15 years, and out of every 1000 who reach the age of 15 years, 950 reach the age of 50 years. Out of every 1000 who reach the age of 50 years, 40 die within one year. What is the probability that a person would attain the age of 51 years?
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must treat survival to each milestone as a chain of conditional probabilities and multiply them: P(reach 15) = 0.9, P(reach 50 | reach 15) = 0.95, P(survive the year after 50 | reach 50) = 1 - 0.04 = 0.96. Full marks require multiplying all three (0.9 x 0.95 x 0.96 = 0.8208) and stating this as the unconditional probability of attaining age 51; partial credit for a correct conditional-probability setup without the final numeric answer.

pyqs.question_text: Let T1 and T2 be two unbiased estimators of theta with Var(T1) = Var(T2). Show that Corr(T1, T2) is greater than or equal to 2e - 1, where e is the efficiency of each estimator.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must consider a convex combination or the average of T1 and T2, use the Cramer-Rao bound to relate its variance to efficiency e, and expand Var((T1+T2)/2) in terms of Var(T1), Var(T2) and Cov(T1,T2). Full marks require correctly showing that non-negativity of this variance combined with the efficiency bound forces Corr(T1,T2) >= 2e-1, with all algebraic steps shown; partial credit for a correct variance expansion without completing the inequality.

pyqs.question_text: Let a random variable X have exponential distribution with mean 1/theta, theta > 0. To test H0: theta = 3 against H1: theta = 2, construct a sequential probability ratio test. Show that the probability of terminating the test at the first stage when the null hypothesis is true is 1 - (8/27)((A-B)/(AB)), where A and B, with B < A, are the stopping bounds.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must set up the likelihood ratio for the exponential density under theta=2 versus theta=3 and define the SPRT continuation region B < likelihood ratio < A. Candidate should derive the boundary values of the first observation x1 at which the test stops, compute the probability of these boundary events under theta=3 (i.e., using the exponential(3) density), and simplify to the stated closed form. Full marks require the complete derivation with correct integration limits; partial credit for correctly setting up the SPRT decision rule without the final simplified probability.

pyqs.question_text: The following data present the time in minutes that a commuter had to wait to catch a bus over 20 days. Use the sign test at 0.05 level of significance to test the claim of the bus operators that commuters do not have to wait for more than 15 minutes before the bus is made available to them. [Given Z(0.025) = 1.96, Z(0.05) = 1.645]
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must state H0: median wait time <= 15 against H1: median > 15, replace each observation by a plus or minus sign according to whether it exceeds 15, and count the number of plus signs among the 20 observations. Full marks require using the normal approximation to the binomial sign-test statistic with continuity correction, comparing the computed Z value against the one-sided critical value 1.645, and stating a clear accept/reject conclusion; partial credit for a correct sign count without completing the test statistic and decision.

pyqs.question_text: Theoretical probabilities in the four cells of a multinomial distribution are (2+theta)/4, (1-theta)/4, (1-theta)/4 and theta/4, whereas the observed frequencies are 108, 27, 30 and 8 respectively. Estimate theta by the maximum likelihood method. Also obtain the standard error of the estimate.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must write the multinomial log-likelihood in theta using the given cell probabilities and observed frequencies, differentiate and set to zero to obtain a quadratic (or simplified linear) equation in theta, and solve for the MLE. Full marks require deriving the Fisher information for theta from the second derivative of the log-likelihood and reporting the standard error as the reciprocal square root of the information evaluated at the MLE; partial credit for a correct likelihood equation without completing the standard-error computation.

pyqs.question_text: Let X be a 3-dimensional random vector with dispersion matrix Sigma having diagonal entries 9 and off-diagonal entries 3. Determine the first principal component and the proportion of the total variability that it explains.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must find the eigenvalues of the given dispersion matrix by exploiting its equicorrelated structure, obtain the largest eigenvalue and its corresponding normalised eigenvector, and write the first principal component as that eigenvector's linear combination of the original variables. Full marks require computing the proportion of total variance explained as the largest eigenvalue divided by the trace of Sigma; partial credit for correct eigenvalues without the normalised eigenvector or the explained-variance ratio.

pyqs.question_text: What do you understand by Statistical Quality Control (SQC)? Discuss briefly its need and utility in industry. Discuss the causes of variation in quality.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer should define SQC as the application of statistical methods to monitor and control a production process, briefly justify its industrial utility in reducing defectives and cost while improving consistency, and then classify causes of variation into chance (random, inherent) causes and assignable (special) causes. Full marks require clearly distinguishing the two types of causes and linking assignable causes to the rationale for control charts; partial credit for a correct definition without the cause classification.

pyqs.question_text: Consider an item with failure rate Z(t) = t/(t+1). Write down the survivor function R(t) and hence evaluate the Mean Time To Failure (MTTF). Also obtain the conditional survival function and Mean Residual Life (MRL).
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must integrate the hazard function Z(t) to obtain the cumulative hazard, then write R(t) = exp(-integral of Z(t)), and integrate R(t) over (0, infinity) to obtain the MTTF. Full marks require correctly forming the conditional survival function R(t+x)/R(t) and integrating it over x to give the Mean Residual Life as a function of t; partial credit for a correct survivor function without completing MTTF or MRL.

pyqs.question_text: Solve the following linear programming problem using the graphical approach: Minimize 4x1 + 5x2 + 6x3 subject to x1 + x2 >= 11, x1 - x2 <= 5, x3 - x1 - x2 = 0, 7x1 + 12x2 >= 35, and x1, x2, x3 >= 0.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate must first use the equality constraint to substitute x3 = x1 + x2, reducing the problem to two variables, then plot the feasible region defined by the remaining inequalities in the x1-x2 plane. Full marks require correctly identifying the feasible region's corner points, evaluating the objective function at each, and selecting the minimum with justification; partial credit for a correctly reduced two-variable problem without a complete graphical solution.

pyqs.question_text: Explain the G/M/1 queuing model and show that the steady-state arrival-point system size distribution is geometric.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must describe the G/M/1 model's general (non-exponential) inter-arrival times with exponential service, and set up the embedded Markov chain at arrival epochs using the transition probabilities involving the number served during an inter-arrival interval. Full marks require deriving the characteristic root of the resulting difference equation and showing the stationary distribution takes the geometric form with that root as the common ratio; partial credit for a correct embedded-chain formulation without deriving the geometric form.

pyqs.question_text: How does the concept of wholesale price index work? Describe the major components of the wholesale price index. Explain the methodology of index numbers of area, production and yield in agriculture.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must explain the wholesale price index as a weighted average of price relatives of a fixed basket of goods traded at the wholesale level, list its major commodity-group components, and describe how base-year weights and current-period prices combine into the index formula. Full marks require then explaining how area, production and yield indices in agriculture are constructed as ratios of current to base-period values aggregated across crops; partial credit for a correct WPI explanation without the agricultural index methodology.

pyqs.question_text: What are the various indices of mortality measure? Explain the purpose and procedure for standardizing them.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Candidate should list crude death rate, age-specific death rates, and standardised death rates as the main mortality indices, explaining why crude rates are misleading when populations differ in age composition. Full marks require describing both direct standardisation (applying a population's age-specific rates to a standard population's age structure) and indirect standardisation, with the purpose of enabling fair mortality comparisons across populations; partial credit for listing the indices without explaining the standardisation procedure.

content_items.title: The Central Limit Theorem and Why It Matters Beyond Normal Populations
content_items.body: The Central Limit Theorem is arguably the single most consequential result in classical statistics because it explains why the normal distribution appears so often in practice even when the underlying population is not normal at all. In its simplest form, the theorem states that if X1, X2, ..., Xn are independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean mu and finite variance sigma-squared, then the standardised sum (or equivalently the standardised sample mean), formed by subtracting n times mu and dividing by sigma times the square root of n, converges in distribution to the standard normal distribution as n grows large. What makes this remarkable is the near-total absence of assumptions about the shape of the parent distribution: whether the underlying variables are binomial, exponential, uniform or badly skewed, their properly scaled sum still settles into a bell-shaped normal curve once enough of them are summed. A classic illustration used in the UPSC Statistics syllabus involves the Poisson distribution: because a Poisson random variable with a large mean can itself be represented as a sum of many independent unit-mean Poisson variables, the CLT can be invoked to show that the Poisson distribution is well approximated by a normal distribution when its mean is large, which is exactly the reasoning behind proving that a certain infinite-sum expression built from Poisson probabilities converges to one half. The theorem's power extends well past this single example. It underlies why sample means of almost any measured quantity, whether examination scores, crop yields, or manufacturing tolerances, tend to be approximately normal even when individual measurements are not, which in turn justifies the widespread use of z-tests and confidence intervals built on normal theory even for non-normal data, provided the sample size is reasonably large. Different versions of the theorem relax the identical-distribution assumption; the Lindeberg-Feller and Liapounov forms allow the summed variables to have different distributions as long as no single term dominates the total variance, which is essential for justifying normal approximations in more realistic, heterogeneous settings such as survey sampling or time series with varying variances. The rate at which convergence to normality occurs is itself of practical interest, and the Berry-Esseen theorem provides an explicit bound on the approximation error in terms of the third absolute moment of the underlying distribution, giving a rough rule of thumb for how large a sample is needed before the normal approximation becomes trustworthy. Taken together, the Central Limit Theorem is what allows statisticians to build a unified inferential framework around the normal distribution despite the enormous diversity of real-world data-generating processes.

content_items.title: Sufficiency, Completeness and the Cramer-Rao Lower Bound
content_items.body: Estimation theory in the UPSC Statistics syllabus builds around a small set of interlocking ideas that together define what it means for an estimator to be good, and sufficiency, completeness and the Cramer-Rao inequality sit at the core of this framework. A statistic T is called sufficient for a parameter theta if the conditional distribution of the sample given T does not depend on theta at all, meaning that T captures every scrap of information the sample carries about theta, so that no further function of the raw data can add anything useful once T is known. The Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem gives a practical way to identify sufficiency: a statistic is sufficient if and only if the joint density of the sample can be factored into a part depending on the data only through T and theta, multiplied by a part depending on the data alone and not on theta. Beyond sufficiency, a statistic is called complete if the only unbiased estimator of zero built from it is the zero function itself; when a sufficient statistic is also complete, the Lehmann-Scheffe theorem guarantees that any unbiased estimator that is a function of this complete sufficient statistic is the unique minimum variance unbiased estimator (MVUE) of the parameter, which is one of the most powerful and widely used results in the entire theory of estimation because it converts a search over all possible unbiased estimators into a much more tractable search restricted to functions of one statistic. Separately, the Cramer-Rao inequality supplies a universal lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator, expressed as the reciprocal of the Fisher information contained in the sample about theta, where Fisher information itself measures the expected curvature of the log-likelihood function and thus how sharply the likelihood distinguishes nearby values of theta. An estimator whose variance actually achieves this lower bound is called efficient, and the ratio of the Cramer-Rao bound to an estimator's actual variance defines its efficiency, a number between zero and one that quantifies how close the estimator comes to the theoretical best possible performance. These three concepts interlock tightly in practice: many textbook problems ask a candidate to verify that a natural estimator, such as a sample mean or a maximum likelihood estimator, is simultaneously sufficient, complete, unbiased and attains the Cramer-Rao bound, thereby proving in one stroke that it is the best possible unbiased estimator available for that model. Mastering the interplay between these ideas is essential preparation for the estimation theory portion of the Statistics optional, since most numerical problems in this area ultimately reduce to identifying sufficiency, checking completeness, or computing and comparing variances against the Cramer-Rao bound.

content_items.title: The Neyman-Pearson Lemma and the Search for Optimal Tests
content_items.body: Hypothesis testing asks a deceptively simple question: given sample data, should a researcher reject a null hypothesis in favour of an alternative, and among the many possible rejection rules, which one is best? The Neyman-Pearson lemma answers this question decisively for the special case of testing one simple hypothesis against another simple alternative, and it forms the theoretical backbone of the entire testing-of-hypotheses portion of the Statistics optional syllabus. A test is defined by its size, the probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis), and its power, the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, and among all tests with a size fixed at some chosen level alpha, the most powerful test is the one that maximises power against the specific alternative under consideration. The Neyman-Pearson lemma states that this most powerful test rejects the null hypothesis whenever the likelihood ratio, the ratio of the likelihood of the data under the alternative hypothesis to its likelihood under the null hypothesis, exceeds some threshold constant k, where k is chosen so that the test has exactly the desired size alpha; a randomised decision rule handles the boundary case where the likelihood ratio equals k exactly, which becomes necessary for discrete distributions where an exact size alpha cannot always be achieved by a deterministic rule. The proof of the lemma is a clean application of a simple inequality argument comparing the performance of the likelihood-ratio test against any other test of the same size, and it is a staple derivation that candidates are expected to reproduce. The lemma's importance extends well beyond the simple-versus-simple case for which it is proved directly, because it motivates the construction of uniformly most powerful (UMP) tests for composite alternatives whenever the underlying family of distributions has a property called monotone likelihood ratio, under which the same likelihood-ratio-based rejection region turns out to be most powerful simultaneously against every value in a one-sided composite alternative. When no UMP test exists, as is common for two-sided alternatives, the theory moves to unbiased tests and eventually to uniformly most powerful unbiased (UMPU) tests, which impose the additional requirement that the test's power never falls below its size for any alternative. The generalised likelihood ratio test extends these ideas further still to composite hypotheses on both sides, using the ratio of the maximised likelihoods under the null and under the unrestricted parameter space as its test statistic, and it underlies many familiar large-sample procedures including the chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Altogether, the Neyman-Pearson framework establishes both the ideal against which all other tests are judged and the conceptual scaffolding from which the entire modern theory of hypothesis testing grew.

content_items.title: Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test
content_items.body: Abraham Wald's sequential probability ratio test, commonly abbreviated SPRT, represents a fundamentally different philosophy of hypothesis testing compared to the classical fixed-sample-size approach, and it occupies an important place in the testing-of-hypotheses section of the Statistics optional syllabus. In a conventional test, the sample size n is decided in advance, all n observations are collected, and only then is a single decision made to accept or reject the null hypothesis. The SPRT instead examines observations one at a time as they arrive and, after each new observation, updates a running likelihood ratio comparing the probability of the observed data so far under the alternative hypothesis to its probability under the null hypothesis. Two boundary constants, conventionally called A and B with B less than A, are fixed in advance based on the desired Type I and Type II error probabilities, and sampling continues only as long as the running likelihood ratio remains strictly between B and A; the moment the ratio rises to or above A, the null hypothesis is rejected, and the moment it falls to or below B, the null hypothesis is accepted, with the test terminating at that point rather than continuing to a predetermined sample size. Wald showed that the boundaries A and B can be approximated very simply in terms of the desired size alpha and desired Type II error probability beta, using A approximately equal to (1-beta)/alpha and B approximately equal to beta/(1-alpha), which makes the procedure straightforward to implement without extensive computation. The central theoretical payoff of the SPRT, established by the Wald-Wolfowitz theorem, is that among all tests (sequential or fixed-sample) achieving the same size and power against the two hypotheses being compared, the SPRT minimises the expected sample size needed to reach a decision, under both the null and the alternative hypothesis; this efficiency gain, often amounting to roughly half the sample size required by an equivalent fixed-sample test, is what has made sequential testing attractive in settings such as industrial quality inspection and clinical trials, where sampling or observation is costly and stopping as early as possible is valuable. A typical syllabus problem asks a candidate to construct the SPRT for a specific parametric family, such as testing one value of the rate parameter of an exponential distribution against another, and then to compute the probability that the test terminates after only the very first observation, which requires expressing the likelihood-ratio boundary crossing condition in terms of the first observation's value and integrating the relevant density over the region where that boundary is crossed. Understanding both the construction of the SPRT and its optimality properties is essential, since questions in this area typically demand a full derivation rather than a statement of the general theory alone.

content_items.title: Principal Component Analysis — Reducing Dimensions Without Losing Information
content_items.body: Principal component analysis, universally abbreviated PCA, is one of the foundational techniques of multivariate analysis covered in Statistics Paper I, and it addresses a very practical problem: when data are recorded on many correlated variables simultaneously, how can that information be compressed into a much smaller number of new variables while discarding as little of the original variability as possible? PCA answers this by constructing new variables, called principal components, as linear combinations of the original variables, chosen so that the first principal component captures the maximum possible variance among all such linear combinations, the second principal component captures the maximum remaining variance subject to being uncorrelated with the first, and so on for successive components. Mathematically, this construction reduces to an eigenvalue problem: if Sigma denotes the variance-covariance (dispersion) matrix of the original variables, the principal components correspond to the eigenvectors of Sigma, and the variance explained by each component equals the corresponding eigenvalue. Because the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix are always non-negative and sum to the total variance (the trace of Sigma), the proportion of total variability explained by any single principal component is simply that component's eigenvalue divided by the trace, which gives a direct and interpretable measure of how much information is retained if only the first few components are kept. A particularly tractable special case that appears repeatedly in examination problems involves an equicorrelated covariance structure, where every variable has the same variance and every pair of variables shares the same covariance; such matrices have a simple, closed-form eigenstructure, with one eigenvalue corresponding to the equally-weighted average of all variables (which typically becomes the first principal component precisely because positive equal correlation concentrates variance into this common direction) and the remaining eigenvalues, all equal to each other, corresponding to contrasts among the variables. Once the components are extracted, practitioners typically retain only enough of them to explain a chosen threshold of total variance, commonly seventy to ninety percent, thereby replacing a large number of correlated original variables with a much smaller number of uncorrelated derived variables suitable for further analysis such as regression or classification without the instability caused by multicollinearity. PCA differs from factor analysis, with which it is often confused, in that PCA is a purely descriptive, distribution-free transformation of the observed variance structure, whereas factor analysis posits an underlying probabilistic model with latent common factors and specific error variances. Within the UPSC syllabus, PCA is grouped alongside other dimension-reduction and relationship-summarising multivariate techniques such as canonical correlation and discriminant analysis, all of which share the common goal of making sense of data recorded simultaneously on many interrelated variables.

content_items.title: Balanced Incomplete Block Designs in Experimental Statistics
content_items.body: The design of experiments portion of the Statistics optional syllabus moves beyond the simplest layouts, such as the completely randomised design and the randomised block design, to handle situations where practical constraints make it impossible to test every treatment within every block, and the balanced incomplete block design, universally abbreviated BIBD, is the classical solution to exactly this problem. A block design is called incomplete when each block contains fewer plots or units than the total number of treatments under study, so that not every treatment can appear in every block, a situation that arises naturally when, for instance, an agricultural field trial has plots too small to accommodate every fertiliser being compared, or a taste-testing panel session is too short for every panelist to evaluate every product. A BIBD imposes a specific balance condition on how treatments are distributed across the incomplete blocks: with v treatments arranged into b blocks of size k each, every treatment appears in exactly r blocks, and, crucially, every pair of distinct treatments appears together in exactly the same number of blocks, denoted lambda. These five parameters are not independent but satisfy two necessary relations that any valid BIBD must obey: vr equals bk (counting the total number of treatment-appearances two different ways), and lambda(v-1) equals r(k-1) (counting, for a fixed treatment, how many times it co-occurs with each of the other v-1 treatments). This built-in balance ensures that every pairwise treatment comparison is estimated with exactly the same precision, which is the entire point of imposing the structure in the first place, since an unbalanced incomplete design would let some treatment comparisons be estimated far more precisely than others purely as an artefact of the layout rather than the underlying science. Analysing data from a BIBD requires a more careful adjustment than an ordinary two-way analysis of variance because block and treatment effects are no longer orthogonal to each other once some treatment-block combinations are simply absent from the data; the standard approach computes adjusted treatment totals that correct for the uneven pattern of block membership before testing for treatment differences via an F-test, and the efficiency of a BIBD relative to a hypothetical complete block design (which would need much larger blocks) is captured by a specific efficiency factor computed from lambda, k and r. BIBDs are widely used wherever resource constraints limit how many treatments a single block, session, or subject can be exposed to, and their mathematical connection to combinatorial design theory, including symmetric BIBDs and their relationship to finite projective planes, makes this topic a natural bridge between applied experimental design and pure combinatorics within the statistics syllabus.

content_items.title: Stratified Random Sampling and the Gain in Precision
content_items.body: Stratified random sampling is among the most widely used probability sampling designs covered in the sampling theory portion of the Statistics optional, and it is built on a simple but powerful idea: when a population can be divided into internally homogeneous subgroups, called strata, sampling separately within each stratum and combining the results almost always yields a more precise estimate of the population total or mean than a simple random sample of the same overall size drawn without regard to this subgroup structure. The procedure begins by partitioning the entire population of N units into L mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive strata based on some auxiliary characteristic known in advance, such as geographic region, farm size class, or industry sector, and then drawing an independent simple random sample from each stratum. The stratified sample mean is formed as a weighted average of the individual stratum sample means, with weights equal to each stratum's share of the total population, and this estimator is unbiased for the overall population mean regardless of how the strata are formed, as long as every unit in the population belongs to exactly one stratum and every stratum is actually sampled. The genuine statistical benefit of stratification lies in its effect on variance: because the variance of the stratified estimator depends only on the variability of units within each stratum, and not at all on the variability between strata, forming strata that are internally as homogeneous as possible (even though the strata may differ substantially from one another) removes the between-stratum variation entirely from the sampling error, producing a variance that is never larger, and typically substantially smaller, than that of simple random sampling with the same total sample size. This principle directly motivates the two classical allocation rules taught alongside stratification: proportional allocation, which assigns each stratum a sample size proportional to its population size and is simple to implement, and Neyman allocation, which assigns each stratum a sample size proportional to the product of its population size and its internal standard deviation, thereby sampling more heavily from strata that are both large and internally variable, and which can be shown to minimise the variance of the stratified estimator for a given total sample size and cost. A further refinement, optimum allocation, generalises Neyman allocation to account for strata that differ in the cost of sampling a unit, balancing precision against budget by allocating more of the sample to strata where information can be gathered more cheaply. Because the gains from stratification depend entirely on how well the chosen stratifying variable predicts the variable actually being measured, choosing a sensible basis for stratification, one correlated with the study variable, is as important in practice as the mathematics of the allocation formulas themselves.

content_items.title: Control Charts and the Statistical Foundations of Process Monitoring
content_items.body: Statistical quality control, a major component of Statistics Paper II under industrial statistics, rests on a foundational distinction between two categories of variation present in any manufacturing or production process: chance causes, which are the many small, unavoidable sources of variability that are always present even when a process is running exactly as intended, and assignable causes, which are specific, identifiable, and in principle correctable sources of variation such as a worn tool, an untrained operator, or a defective batch of raw material. A process is said to be in a state of statistical control when only chance causes are operating, producing output that varies randomly but predictably around a stable mean, and the control chart, developed originally by Walter Shewhart, is the primary tool used to detect the moment an assignable cause enters the process and disturbs this stable pattern. A typical control chart plots a sample statistic, such as the sample mean (in an X-bar chart) or the sample range (in an R-chart), against time or sample number, together with a horizontal centre line at the process's target or estimated mean value and two horizontal control limits, conventionally placed three standard errors of the plotted statistic above and below the centre line. As long as successive plotted points fall within these three-sigma limits and show no systematic non-random pattern, the process is judged to be in control; a point falling outside the limits, or certain non-random patterns of points within the limits such as a long run on one side of the centre line, signals that an assignable cause is likely present and warrants investigation and correction. The X-bar and R-chart pair is used together specifically because the X-bar chart alone monitors the process mean while the R-chart monitors process variability, and both must be in control simultaneously for the process as a whole to be considered stable; the control limits for both charts are computed from tabulated constants (commonly denoted A2, D3 and D4) that depend on the sample size used for each subgroup, derived from the theoretical relationship between the range and the standard deviation of a normal distribution. Beyond monitoring, control chart data also feed into an assessment of process capability, which compares the natural spread of a controlled process (typically six standard deviations wide) against the width of the engineering specification limits the product must meet, producing capability indices that quantify whether a process that is merely in statistical control is also capable of reliably producing acceptable output. Control charts thus serve a dual purpose central to industrial statistics: detecting departures from stability in real time, and providing the baseline data needed to judge whether a stable process is actually good enough for its intended purpose.

content_items.title: Reliability Analysis and the Idea of the Failure Rate Function
content_items.body: Reliability theory, covered under industrial statistics in Statistics Paper II, studies the length of time a component, system or item functions before it fails, and it builds its entire mathematical apparatus around a small number of interrelated functions describing the lifetime random variable T. The survivor function R(t), defined as the probability that the item survives beyond time t, starts at one when t is zero and decreases monotonically to zero as t grows large, providing the most direct summary of an item's longevity. Closely related is the failure rate function, also called the hazard function and denoted Z(t) or h(t), defined as the instantaneous rate of failure at time t given survival up to that time; formally it equals the probability density function of T divided by the survivor function R(t), and it can be interpreted as the conditional probability of failing in the next small instant given the item has lasted this long. Because R(t) can be recovered from Z(t) by integrating the hazard function and exponentiating its negative cumulative value, specifying either function is mathematically equivalent to specifying the other, and much of reliability analysis consists of choosing a hazard function shape that matches the physical failure mechanism of interest: a constant hazard rate corresponds to the memoryless exponential lifetime distribution typical of electronic components failing due to random shocks, while an increasing hazard rate, as seen in mechanical wear-out, is often modelled using a Weibull distribution with shape parameter greater than one. Two summary measures derived from these functions are of central practical importance: the Mean Time To Failure, or MTTF, is simply the expected value of the lifetime T and can be computed directly as the integral of the survivor function R(t) over its entire range from zero to infinity, providing a single number describing average longevity; and the Mean Residual Life, or MRL, generalises this idea to items that have already survived to some age t, defined as the expected remaining lifetime given survival to time t, computed as the integral of the conditional survival function R(t+x)/R(t) over the remaining time x. The behaviour of MRL as a function of age carries important engineering meaning: a constant MRL again characterises the exponential distribution's memoryless property, a decreasing MRL indicates that older items are expected to fail sooner (consistent with wear-out), and an increasing MRL, though less intuitive, can arise in certain systems where surviving early hazards is informative of underlying robustness. These reliability functions together provide the mathematical language used throughout the syllabus for analysing censored life-testing data, comparing competing product designs, and setting warranty periods based on acceptable failure probabilities.

content_items.title: Two-Person Zero-Sum Games and the Minimax Principle
content_items.body: Game theory enters the Statistics optional syllabus as part of optimisation techniques because it provides a rigorous framework for decision-making in competitive situations, and the two-person zero-sum game is the simplest and most thoroughly developed model within this framework. In such a game, two players, conventionally called A and B, each choose one of a finite set of available strategies, and the resulting payoff to player A (with the corresponding loss to player B, since the total is always zero) is recorded in a payoff matrix whose rows correspond to A's strategies and whose columns correspond to B's strategies. Player A, who wants to maximise the guaranteed payoff, reasons defensively by considering the worst outcome (the minimum payoff) associated with each of A's own strategies and then choosing the strategy that makes this worst-case outcome as large as possible, a rule called the maximin principle; symmetrically, player B, who wants to minimise A's payoff, considers the best outcome (from A's perspective, the maximum) associated with each of B's strategies and chooses to make this best-case outcome as small as possible, the minimax principle. When the resulting maximin value (the largest of the row minimums) equals the minimax value (the smallest of the column maximums), the game is said to have a saddle point, and this common value is called the value of the game; at a saddle point, neither player can improve their outcome by unilaterally switching strategies, so both players have an optimal pure strategy that they should play with certainty every time the game is repeated. Many realistic games, however, have no saddle point, meaning the maximin value falls strictly below the minimax value, and in this situation pure strategies are no longer adequate; instead, each player must adopt a mixed strategy, playing each of their available pure strategies with some pre-determined probability, chosen so as to guarantee an expected payoff regardless of what the opponent does. For a simple two-by-two payoff matrix without a saddle point, the optimal mixed strategy probabilities and the resulting value of the game can be obtained directly using a straightforward algebraic formula derived from equalising the expected payoff against either of the opponent's pure strategies; larger games are typically solved either graphically, when one player has only two strategies, or by reformulating the game as an equivalent linear programming problem, since the fundamental duality between a two-person zero-sum game and a pair of dual linear programs is one of the deepest connections between game theory and optimisation. This linkage means that the simplex method and other linear programming solution techniques taught elsewhere in the optimisation portion of the syllabus can be applied directly to solve games too large to handle by elementary algebraic or graphical methods.

content_items.title: Queuing Theory and the Classical M/M/1 Waiting-Line Model
content_items.body: Queuing theory, taught under optimisation techniques in Statistics Paper II, provides the mathematical machinery for analysing systems in which customers, jobs, or items arrive over time to be served by a limited number of servers, and must sometimes wait when the server is busy. The simplest and most extensively studied model is the M/M/1 queue, whose name follows Kendall's notation: the first M indicates that arrivals follow a Markovian (memoryless) process, specifically a Poisson process with constant arrival rate lambda; the second M indicates that service times are also Markovian, meaning exponentially distributed with constant service rate mu; and the 1 indicates a single server. Because both the inter-arrival times and service times are memoryless, the number of customers present in the system at any moment forms a continuous-time Markov chain, called a birth-death process, in which the population size increases by one at each arrival and decreases by one at each service completion. When the traffic intensity rho, defined as lambda divided by mu, is strictly less than one, meaning the server can on average clear customers faster than they arrive, the system reaches a steady state in which the probability of finding n customers in the system settles down to a geometric distribution with parameter rho, specifically P(n customers) equals (1 minus rho) times rho raised to the power n; the requirement that rho be less than one is essential, since a system where arrivals exceed service capacity would see the queue grow without bound and never reach any steady state at all. From this steady-state distribution, several performance measures of direct practical interest can be derived: the expected number of customers in the system equals rho divided by (1 minus rho), the expected number waiting in the queue (excluding the one currently being served) equals rho-squared divided by (1 minus rho), and, through Little's Law, which relates the average number in a system to the average arrival rate and the average time spent in the system, the expected waiting time and expected time in the system follow directly from the expected queue lengths. The M/G/1 model relaxes the assumption of exponential service times to allow a general service-time distribution while retaining Poisson arrivals, and its steady-state behaviour is captured by the well-known Pollaczek-Khinchine formula for the expected queue length, which reduces exactly to the M/M/1 result when the general service distribution happens to be exponential. The G/M/1 model instead relaxes the arrival process to a general renewal process while keeping exponential service, and its steady-state distribution, examined at the specific instants when customers arrive, again turns out to be geometric, though with its ratio parameter determined implicitly by a transform equation rather than the simple explicit ratio rho used in M/M/1. These models collectively give planners of banks, telecommunications networks, hospital emergency rooms and manufacturing lines a rigorous way to predict congestion and to decide how many servers or what service capacity is needed to keep waiting times within acceptable bounds.

content_items.title: Index Numbers and the Measurement of Price Change
content_items.body: Index numbers form a core part of quantitative economics and official statistics in Statistics Paper II, and they solve a deceptively difficult measurement problem: how does one summarise the overall change in the price (or quantity) of a large basket of heterogeneous goods, such as an entire economy's consumption bundle, into a single comparable number over time? A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket of goods in a given (current) period against its cost in a chosen base period, expressed conventionally as a ratio multiplied by one hundred so that the base period always reads exactly 100. The simplest construction, Laspeyres' price index, values the basket using base-period quantities as fixed weights, which has the practical advantage of not requiring updated quantity information every period but tends to overstate inflation over time because it does not allow for consumers substituting away from goods that have become relatively more expensive. Paasche's price index instead uses current-period quantities as weights, correcting this substitution bias but requiring fresh quantity data each period and tending, for the opposite reason, to understate the true cost-of-living increase. Fisher's ideal index, defined as the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices, is often preferred theoretically because it satisfies several desirable mathematical properties, including the time-reversal test (the index computed from period 0 to period 1 should be the reciprocal of the index computed from period 1 to period 0) and the factor-reversal test, neither of which the Laspeyres or Paasche index satisfies individually. In practical official statistics, India's Wholesale Price Index (WPI) tracks price movements of goods at the wholesale or producer level, aggregating price relatives of a fixed basket of commodities grouped into primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products, each carrying a fixed weight reflecting its importance in wholesale trade during a chosen base year, and the index is used chiefly to monitor inflation from the production side of the economy. A parallel but conceptually distinct family of index numbers is used in agricultural statistics to track area, production and yield: an area index compares the total cropped area of a commodity (or basket of commodities) in the current period to the base period; a production index compares total output similarly; and a yield index, since yield equals production divided by area, is mathematically linked to the other two, so that the production index can always be decomposed into the product of the area index and the yield index, a relationship that helps analysts determine whether a change in agricultural output stemmed mainly from expanded cultivation or from productivity improvement. Together, these index-number techniques provide the standard toolkit through which national statistical agencies translate raw price and quantity data into the summary indicators, such as inflation rates and agricultural growth rates, that inform economic policy.

content_items.title: Life Tables and the Measurement of Mortality
content_items.body: The life table is one of the oldest and most enduring tools of demographic and actuarial statistics, and it forms the centrepiece of the vital-statistics portion of the Demography and Psychometry section of Statistics Paper II. A life table follows a hypothetical cohort of some fixed initial number of individuals, conventionally denoted l0 (often taken as 100,000), as it is progressively reduced by mortality at each successive age, recording at every age x the number of survivors lx, the number dying between age x and x+1 denoted dx (so that dx equals lx minus l(x+1)), and the probability of dying within the year following age x given survival to age x, denoted qx and computed as dx divided by lx; the complementary survival probability px equals one minus qx. From these basic columns, a life table builds further quantities of central demographic interest, most importantly ex, the expectation of life at age x, which represents the average number of additional complete years a person aged x may expect to live, computed using the total person-years lived by the cohort beyond age x divided by the number of survivors at age x. Because raw death counts are heavily influenced by a population's age structure (a population with disproportionately many elderly residents will naturally show more deaths than a young population even if age-specific mortality risks are identical in both), demographers rarely rely on the crude death rate, the simple ratio of total deaths to total population in a year, for comparing mortality across populations or over time. Instead, they compute age-specific death rates for narrow age bands and then combine these into a single comparable figure through standardisation: direct standardisation applies the age-specific death rates observed in the population being studied to the age structure of an agreed standard population, producing a standardised death rate that reflects what mortality would have looked like had the study population possessed the standard age distribution, while indirect standardisation instead applies the age-specific rates of a standard population to the study population's own age structure, producing a standardised mortality ratio comparing observed to expected deaths, a technique especially useful when a study population's own age-specific rates are based on very small numbers and therefore unreliable. A subtle but important relationship taught alongside these ideas links ex, the mortality probability qx, and the population's structure between consecutive ages: because a person's remaining lifetime beyond age x depends jointly on the chance of dying within the coming year and the further life expectancy of those who survive that year, ex, ex+1 and qx satisfy an identity that can be derived directly from the definitions of the life-table functions, and deriving or manipulating such identities is a common examination exercise testing whether a candidate genuinely understands the life-table framework rather than merely memorising its formulas. Life tables underpin far more than academic demography, feeding directly into pension-fund actuarial calculations, health-policy planning, and international comparisons of a population's overall mortality experience.

content_items.title: The Logistic Model of Population Growth
content_items.body: Among the mathematical models of population growth studied under demography and psychometry in Statistics Paper II, the logistic growth curve holds a special place because it corrects a glaring weakness of the simpler exponential growth model while remaining analytically tractable. The exponential model assumes a population grows at a rate strictly proportional to its current size, which produces unbounded growth that no real biological or human population can sustain indefinitely given finite resources, space, and food supply. The logistic model instead assumes that the population's growth rate declines as the population approaches some upper limit L, called the carrying capacity, representing the maximum population size the environment can sustainably support; formally, the growth rate is modelled as proportional both to the current population size and to the remaining unused capacity (L minus the current population), which produces growth that is nearly exponential when the population is small relative to L but which slows and eventually levels off as the population approaches L. Solving the resulting differential equation yields the classical logistic function, expressed as P(t) equal to L divided by (1 plus e raised to the power r(beta minus t)), where L is the carrying capacity, r is a growth-rate parameter controlling how quickly the population moves from near zero toward L, and beta is a location parameter marking the time at which the population reaches exactly half of the carrying capacity. This function traces out the characteristic S-shaped, or sigmoid, curve: growth starts slowly, accelerates through an inflection point located precisely at population size L/2 and time t equal to beta, and then decelerates as the curve flattens toward the asymptote L. Three properties of the logistic curve are typically highlighted in the syllabus: first, the curve is symmetric about its inflection point, so the pattern of growth before reaching half the carrying capacity mirrors the pattern of deceleration after it; second, the curve has two horizontal asymptotes, approaching zero as t goes to negative infinity and approaching L as t goes to positive infinity, meaning the model always predicts eventual stabilisation rather than either extinction or unbounded growth; and third, the instantaneous growth rate itself, when plotted against population size, traces a downward-opening parabola that peaks exactly at the inflection point, reflecting the fact that absolute growth is fastest when the population is at half its eventual maximum, not when it is largest. Beyond its use in modelling national and world population trajectories, where it has historically been fitted to census data with reasonable success over limited time horizons, the same logistic functional form appears throughout the natural and social sciences, describing phenomena from the adoption of new technologies to the spread of epidemics, wherever growth is constrained by a finite ceiling rather than continuing indefinitely.
